stem: A 70 year old female patient presents with severe acute abdominal pain, her ECG shows atrial fibrillation. Basic labs are as follows: WBC: 24×109, Hb: 12 g/dl, PLT: 150×103, Lactate: 8 Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: Source note (Midterm 442 A Q4): Related source finding: CT scan revealed pneumatosis intestinalis. A. Bowel ischemia A
expl: AF (embolic source), severe pain, leukocytosis and lactate 8 → acute bowel (mesenteric) ischaemia.

why.A: SMA syndrome is duodenal compression after weight loss.
why.C: Torsion doesn't fit AF/lactate 8 in a 70-year-old.
why.D: Diverticulitis gives LIF pain and fever without such lactate.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a pulsatile mass behind his right knee. What is the most significant potential complication of this condition?

opts.t: Deep vein thrombosis due to venous compression

expl: A popliteal aneurysm (pulsatile mass behind the knee) mainly thromboses and throws distal emboli → acute limb ischaemia with poor limb salvage. Rupture is rare.

why.A: Rupture is uncommon in limb aneurysms (it is the danger in aortic aneurysms).
why.B: Compression occurs but is less significant.
why.D: Venous compression occurs but is less significant.

stem: A 65-year-old male in the ICU for septic shock develops sudden abdominal pain, distension, and mild lactic acidosis. He is hemodynamically unstable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: Source note (Midterm 439 A Q32): The related ICU/vasopressor recall uses: B. Non-obstructive superior mesenteric ischemia (NOSMI) B
expl: Septic shock on vasopressors + abdominal pain, distension and lactic acidosis = non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia (low-flow splanchnic vasoconstriction).

why.A: Sudden pain in AF/embolic source, out of proportion.

stem: A patient presents after penetrating trauma to the extremity. On examination, which of the following findings is considered a hard sign of vascular injury, requiring emergent surgical exploration?
expl: Hard signs of vascular injury: pulsatile bleeding, expanding haematoma, palpable thrill/audible bruit, absent pulses with ischaemia → surgery without further imaging.

why.A: A stable haematoma is a soft sign.
why.B: An absent pulse alone is debated, but pulsatile bleeding/expanding haematoma is the classic hard sign.
why.D: A nerve deficit is a soft sign.

stem: A 30-year-old male presents with a penetrating thigh injury. On examination, he has a hematoma at the site of injury, but it is not expanding, there is no active bleeding, and his distal pulses are palpable but slightly weak. He is hemodynamically stable and has no neurological deficits. What is the most appropriate next step?
srcNote: BorC not sure The source marks B or C as uncertain; its original key is retained.
expl: The source had no key ("B or C"). Soft signs only (non-expanding haematoma, slightly weak pulses) in a stable patient → CT angiography to exclude arterial injury (ABI < 0.9 also prompts imaging). Hard signs would mean surgery.

why.C: Serial exams alone are acceptable only with normal pulses/ABI.

stem: A 70-year-old man has a history of temporary right-hand weakness for 1-hour last week and carotid bruit on physical examination. Carotid duplex showed 80% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. What is the most likely clinical presentation related to internal carotid artery stenosis?
expl: Symptomatic carotid stenosis presents with transient ischaemic attacks (focal deficit < 24 h — here contralateral hand weakness from a LEFT ICA lesion), amaurosis fugax or stroke, from emboli.

stem: A 55 year old female patient was admitted 2 days ago to CCU with acute myocardial infarction and atrial fibrillation. You were called at midnight because she developed sudden right leg pain and numbness. She has pale right leg palpable right femoral pulse and absent pulses downwards. Her left leg pulses are all palpable. Which ONE of the following is an appropriate next step in management?
expl: Sudden pale painful leg with an embolic source (AF after MI), femoral pulse present and absent distal pulses → acute embolic occlusion at the femoral bifurcation → heparin + urgent Fogarty embolectomy.

why.A: ABI delays treatment of a threatened limb.
why.B: Not needed — the clinical picture localizes the embolus; don't delay.
why.D: Restoring rhythm doesn't remove the embolus.

stem: Which artery of the gastrointestinal tract if thrombosed will cause ischemia in Jejunum, ilium & cecum?
srcNote: Only three answer choices are supplied in the source.
expl: Jejunum, ileum and caecum are midgut — supplied by the SMA.

stem: Which parts of the gastrointestinal tract will be ischemic in case of thrombosis of the superior mesenteric artery?
expl: The SMA supplies the midgut: small intestine (jejunum, ileum), caecum, appendix, ascending colon and proximal ⅔ of the transverse colon.

stem: clinical presentation of acute (it was Critical) limb ischemia
srcNote: or (A if it was critical) ( Peripheral arterial disease) critical limb ischemia presentation (rest pain, gangrene & ulcer) Acute limb ischemia presentation (pain, pallor, poikilothermia, pulselessness, paresthesia, and paralysis) The source is uncertain whether the question asked about acute or critical limb ischemia; both original key possibilities are retained.
expl: Paralysis (motor loss) is the late, severe P of acute limb ischaemia — it signals a threatened limb needing immediate revascularization.

why.A: Toe gangrene is chronic limb-threatening ischaemia.
why.D: Swelling follows reperfusion (compartment syndrome), not the presentation.

stem: Local complication of angiogram and angioplasty?
srcNote: (local: pseudoanyeurysm, systemic: contrast induced nephropathy & anaphylaxis)
expl: Local access-site complications of angiography: hematoma, pseudoaneurysm, AV fistula, dissection, thrombosis. Systemic ones: contrast nephropathy and anaphylaxis.

stem: A 60 year old male presented to ER for sudden left leg pain. History and physicals were taken and was diagnosed with acute limb ischemia. What is the most appropriate treatment?
expl: Acute limb ischaemia → immediate systemic heparin (prevent propagation) + urgent revascularization (embolectomy, thrombolysis or bypass).

why.C: Warfarin is too slow and isn't treatment.

stem: what is the presentation of chronic mesenteric ischemia?
srcNote: Choices B-D are question-mark placeholders in the source.
expl: Chronic mesenteric ischaemia ("intestinal angina") = postprandial abdominal pain → fear of eating → weight loss.

stem: A 45-year-old man presented to the hospital with acute left leg ischemia secondary to trauma After revascularization, the patient should be observed for potential complication. Which complication is most likely to occur secondary to reperfusion syndrome?
expl: Reperfusion of an ischaemic limb washes potassium, lactic acid and myoglobin from dead muscle into the circulation → hyperkalaemia (arrhythmias), metabolic acidosis, myoglobinuric renal failure, plus compartment syndrome. (The source writes "Ans. A".)

stem: An 80 years old man was presented to the ER department with a history of severe abdominal pain of 16 hours associated with diarrhea and vomiting. He is -known case atrial fibrillation and congestive heart failure presently on digoxin. On examination abdomen is distended with guarding and rectum is empty. WBC count 28*10 and abdominal plain x-ray shows edema of the bowel. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management?
srcNote: Source key was D; corrected — see explanation. (Acute Abdomen) Source keys conflict for the same clinical scenario. No replacement answer has been inferred. Other source key (Final 435 F Q44 (p. 151)): D. Antibiotic therapy with ciprofloxacin Ans: D Other source key (Final 433 A Q36 (p. 184)): A. Heparinization. A
expl: An elderly patient with AF and digoxin (vasoconstrictor), severe pain, distension, guarding, WBC 28 and bowel-wall oedema has acute mesenteric ischaemia with peritonitis (likely infarcted bowel) → resuscitate, heparinize and take to theatre for exploration/resection. The source keys conflicted (antibiotics; heparin) — neither treats dead bowel.

why.A: Heparin is given, but peritonitis needs surgery.
why.C: Embolization is for bleeding, not ischaemia.
why.D: Antibiotics alone don't treat infarcted bowel.

stem: A 55-year-old man presented to the hospital with acute left leg ischemia. Which one of the following is the most common cause of acute lower limb Ischemia?
srcNote: (Vascular Emergencies) Here it’s saying “From” Source note (Final 434 A Q26 (p. 162)): Choice A is written as "Embolization to the heart." The source note says: "if one of the choices is Embolization From the heart then it is the correct answer". The original source still marks A.
expl: The most common cause of acute lower-limb ischaemia in the lecture is embolism from the heart (AF, MI) — ~80% of emboli are cardiogenic.

why.B: Thrombosis on atherosclerosis is also common, but the lecture's answer is cardiac embolism.

stem: What is the most concerning symptom in acute limb ischemia?
expl: Sensory loss (paraesthesia) means nerve ischaemia — nerves are the most sensitive tissue — and signals a threatened limb that needs urgent revascularization; paralysis follows.

stem: A 72-year-old diabetic man presented to the ER complaining of lower abdominal pain, nausea and bloody diarrhea for 2 days. Physical examination revealed tenderness in the left lower quadrant. Blood pressure 110/65 mmHg Heart rate 85 /min Temperature 38.2 Respiratory rate 18/min Test Result Normal value WBC 17.4 4-10.5 x 10 9 L Plain abdominal x-ray: thickened descending and sigmoid colon with thumb printing appearance. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Elderly diabetic, LLQ pain, bloody diarrhoea, leukocytosis, and thumb-printing (submucosal oedema/haemorrhage) of the descending/sigmoid colon (watershed) → ischaemic colitis.

why.A: Diverticulitis gives LLQ pain and fever but not bloody diarrhoea with thumb-printing.
why.B: UC starts in the rectum in younger patients.

stem: A 25 year old man is brought to the hospital after a gunshot wound to the right arm approximately 15 minutes prior to arrival. Which of the following findings on a physical exam suggest the presence of an arterial injury requiring urgent angiography or surgical intervention?

opts.t: Proximity of the injury to major vascular structure

srcNote: Source note (Midterm 431 A Q25): (according to lawrence page 209) diminished pulses are considered soft signs which suggest vascular injury
expl: Keyed diminished distal pulses — a sign of arterial injury needing angiography/intervention (soft sign per Lawrence; hard if absent). Hypotension, nerve injury and proximity are non-specific.

why.D: Proximity alone is a weak soft sign.

stem: A 60 y/o female patient, who is known to have ischemic heart disease and diabetes mellitus presents with acute abdomen pain. Her ECG shows arterial fibrillation. An initial impression of acute abdomen is made and patient admitted for further investigations. Which of the following is most likely to reveal her underlying diagnosis?
expl: Keyed: elderly with IHD, DM and AF + acute abdomen → CT (CT angiography) for mesenteric ischaemia and other causes.

why.B: US can't assess mesenteric vessels well.
why.C: Dipstick doesn't assess an acute abdomen.

stem: when examining a patient, you heard a bruit in his carotids what’s to do next:
expl: Keyed "auscultate the precordium": a murmur from aortic stenosis can radiate to the neck and mimic a carotid bruit, so listen to the heart first. If a true carotid bruit remains, carotid duplex ultrasound is the investigation.

why.D: Duplex is the test for a confirmed carotid bruit — reasonable, but the key chose excluding a cardiac source first.
